options.text: The inheritance of characteristics from only one parent
The inheritance of a single characteristic controlled by one gene
The inheritance of sex-linked characteristics
The inheritance of two different characteristics at the same time

questions.explanation: Monohybrid inheritance involves the inheritance of a single characteristic controlled by one gene with two alleles. For example, studying how tongue-rolling ability (one gene) is passed from parents to offspring.

questions.stem: If two heterozygous parents (Bb x Bb) are crossed, what ratio of phenotypes is expected in the offspring?

options.text: All dominant phenotype
All recessive phenotype
3 dominant : 1 recessive
1 dominant : 1 recessive

questions.explanation: When two heterozygous parents (Bb x Bb) are crossed, the expected phenotype ratio is 3 dominant : 1 recessive (3:1). The genotype ratio is 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb. This is the classic Mendelian ratio.

questions.stem: What is a Punnett square used for?

options.text: To count the number of chromosomes in a cell
To determine the DNA sequence of a gene
To predict the possible genotypes and phenotypes of offspring from a cross
To identify mutations in genes

questions.explanation: A Punnett square is a diagram used to predict the possible genotypes and phenotypes of offspring from a genetic cross. It shows all possible combinations of alleles from both parents and the probability of each outcome.

questions.stem: If one parent is homozygous dominant (BB) and the other is homozygous recessive (bb), what will the offspring be?

options.text: All BB
All bb
All Bb
Half BB and half bb

questions.explanation: When BB is crossed with bb, all offspring receive one B allele from one parent and one b allele from the other, making them all Bb (heterozygous). They all show the dominant phenotype but carry the recessive allele.

questions.stem: Two parents who are both carriers (Bb) of a recessive disorder have a child. What is the probability the child will be affected?

options.text: 0 (impossible)

questions.explanation: From a Bb x Bb cross, the possible offspring are BB, Bb, Bb, and bb. Only bb shows the recessive disorder, giving a 1 in 4 (25%) chance. Each child has this same probability, regardless of the phenotypes of previous children.

options.text: Crossing an organism of unknown genotype with a homozygous recessive organism
Testing whether an organism has a mutation
Crossing two organisms that are both homozygous dominant
Crossing two organisms from different species

questions.explanation: A test cross involves crossing an organism showing the dominant phenotype (unknown genotype, either BB or Bb) with a homozygous recessive organism (bb). If any offspring show the recessive phenotype, the unknown parent must be Bb.

questions.stem: Why might actual offspring ratios differ from the predicted ratios in a genetic cross?

options.text: Because the Punnett square is always wrong
Because all offspring must have the same genotype
Because Mendel's laws do not apply to humans
Because fertilisation is random, and predicted ratios are probabilities, not certainties

questions.explanation: Predicted ratios are based on probability. Which sperm fertilises which egg is random, so actual results may differ from expected ratios, especially with small numbers of offspring. With larger samples, actual ratios get closer to predicted ones.
